report.source_text: She underwent further investigation with magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis which demonstrated a tangle of vessels in the right adnexal/pararectal region at approximately the level of the mid to lower rectum with feeding vessels identified from the right internal iliac artery. A few smaller feeding vessels were also identified from the inferior mesenteric and superior rectal arteries. The draining veins were predominantly seen coursing to the right internal iliac vein with a few traced into the left internal iliac vein. The vessels were seen to course the rectal wall on the right lateral aspect without definite luminal invagination. Prominent adnexal vessels were seen bilaterally attributing to background pelvic congestion.

report.source_text: She underwent embolisation with access via the left common femoral artery. There was a small distal right superior rectal AVM with filling of a large right rectal haemorrhoid. This was microcanulated to within 1 cm of the fistula point and embolised with 0.1 mL of N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA) lipiodol. A flexible sigmoidoscopy a few days later demonstrated no features of recent haemorrhage, and a proctoscopy visualised a moderate sized internal haemorrhoid at 7 o'clock which was banded without complications. She was discharged home the next day.

clinician.trajectory_summary: A 17-year-old female presented with 2 days of per rectal bleeding and mild mid-abdominal discomfort. Physical examination revealed epigastric and peri-umbilical tenderness with bright red blood on digital rectal examination, but she was hemodynamically stable. Initial labs showed normal hemoglobin, platelets, and INR. A CT mesenteric angiogram demonstrated prominent serpiginous vessels in the pelvis, highly suggestive of a pelvic AVM, with no active gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Subsequent MRI of the pelvis further characterized the AVM, identifying a tangle of vessels in the right adnexal/pararectal region with feeding vessels from the right internal iliac artery, inferior mesenteric, and superior rectal arteries, and draining into the internal iliac veins. Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) confirmed a right-sided AVM affecting the rectum, noting associated right-sided hemorrhoids due to venous hypertension. The patient underwent embolisation of a distal right superior rectal AVM. Post-embolisation, flexible sigmoidoscopy showed no recent hemorrhage, and a proctoscopy identified and banded a moderate-sized internal hemorrhoid. She was discharged home the next day.
